# AI governance has moved from policy debate to control evidence

[VISUAL: Heading slide. “AI governance is becoming control evidence.” Source: Agentic GRC]

If artificial intelligence agents start acting inside critical infrastructure, will governance look like a new AI rulebook, or like evidence inside the controls operators already run?

[VISUAL: Slide with quote. “Consider the risks these tools pose when evaluating BES Cyber Systems.” Source: FERC via Industrial Cyber]

## The shift

The important change is not that autonomous agents are suddenly running the grid, water systems or transport networks.

The change is that artificial intelligence is being pulled into existing critical-infrastructure governance.

In the United States power sector, Industrial Cyber reported that Federal Energy Regulatory Commission staff flagged access-control risks from “super intelligence” tools, including chatbots, personal assistants and automated analytical systems, as they become embedded in networks supporting Critical Infrastructure Protection assets. [01-c1]

Those Critical Infrastructure Protection rules, often called CIP, govern cyber controls for the Bulk Electric System, or BES.

FERC’s point, as reported, was not that the rules explicitly allow or ban these tools.

It was that entities should consider the risks from these tools when evaluating Bulk Electric System cyber systems and apply appropriate controls. [01-c5]

For executives, that moves the question from, “Do we have an AI policy?” to, “Can we show who or what has access, what system category applies, what monitoring exists, and who is accountable?” [01-c5]

[VISUAL: Slide with heading. “AI infrastructure becomes a reliability issue.” Source: Utility Dive / NERC]

## Data centers as grid actors

A second development is about artificial intelligence infrastructure itself.

Utility Dive reported that North American Electric Reliability Corporation stakeholders approved proposed reliability standards for AI data centers, crypto mining facilities and other large computational loads. [01-c2]

That approval is an important step toward finalization, not the same as full final adoption. [01-c2]

The proposed standards are designed to give transmission operators, balancing authorities and reliability coordinators the computational-load data they need to plan, monitor and assess reliable bulk-power operation. [01-c5]

They also aim to establish communications capabilities and predefined communications protocols so grid operators can act quickly when those loads could affect reliability. [01-c5]

So here again, AI is not being treated only as a software ethics question.

It is being translated into load data, communications paths, operational visibility and reliability obligations. [01-c5]

[VISUAL: Slide with heading. “Threat models now include AI-assisted activity.” Source: MITRE via Industrial Cyber]

## Threat modeling catches up

The third development is in detection and threat modeling.

Industrial Cyber reported that MITRE ATT&CK, MITRE’s public knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques, added campaigns involving attacks on more than 30 Minnesota water and wastewater utilities. [01-c3]

The same update also added an AI-assisted breach of Mexican government infrastructure that crossed from information technology into operational technology and reached a municipal water utility. [01-c3]

MITRE also expanded enterprise coverage for techniques such as prompt injection, AI-enabled data exfiltration, AI result poisoning and attacks targeting AI-assisted defenses. [01-c5]

That matters because operators do not only govern AI through policy.

They also govern it through detection logic, incident playbooks, monitoring analytics and cross-domain visibility between information technology and operational technology. [01-c5]

This does not prove that every critical-infrastructure attacker is now using AI in operational environments.

It does show that major threat-modeling frameworks are beginning to represent AI-assisted activity that crosses the information-technology and operational-technology boundary. [01-c3]

[VISUAL: Slide with quote. “This year, we have that view and it’s real.” Source: Dragos]

## What is real, and what is still uncertain

There is also a practitioner view from Dragos, an operational-technology security company.

In a September video, Dragos said it had avoided claiming real offensive or defensive AI use cases in operational technology until it saw them in the field, and that in 2026 it now sees AI as real for defenders. [01-c4]

That is a company claim, not independent proof of systemic prevalence. [01-c4]

Dragos has commercial incentives, and its statement should be treated as field interpretation from a vendor-practitioner, not as sector-wide incident data. [01-c4]

Still, it points in the same direction as the regulatory and framework evidence.

The visible governance response is narrower than broad “AI safety” language.

It is about authorized access, asset categorization, communications paths, detection analytics, modeling data and accountable operators. [01-c5]

That is my interpretation of the evidence across FERC, North American Electric Reliability Corporation developments and MITRE ATT&CK updates. [01-c5]

[VISUAL: Closing slide. “What to watch: controls, standards, evidence.” Source: Agentic GRC]

## What to watch

Watch whether FERC audit lessons turn into repeat findings or clearer expectations for AI-like tools in Critical Infrastructure Protection environments.

Watch whether the North American Electric Reliability Corporation standards for AI data centers and other computational loads move from stakeholder approval to enforceable reliability requirements. [01-c2]

Watch whether MITRE ATT&CK and similar frameworks keep adding AI-assisted techniques that affect operational technology, water, energy and other critical infrastructure. [01-c3]

And watch your own evidence.

For boards and executives, the practical test is not whether an AI policy exists.

It is whether the operator can prove what the AI system can reach, what it can change, how it is monitored, and who is responsible when it acts. [01-c5]
